title: Indonesian Diaspora Abroad: Your Complete Guide to Thriving Overseas
summary: Everything the Indonesian diaspora abroad needs to know: from moving overseas and building a community to sending money home and staying connected to roots.
body_markdown:
[Living Abroad](https://blog.transfez.com/en/living-abroad/)


So you are thinking about packing your bags and building a new life overseas. Or maybe you have already made the leap and are now somewhere between excited and completely overwhelmed. Either way, you are not alone. The **Indonesian diaspora abroad** is one of the most vibrant and fast-growing communities in the world, with millions of Indonesians living, working, and studying across Asia, Europe, the Middle East, Australia, and beyond. And if you want a full picture of what that journey really looks like, the[Indonesian Diaspora Living Abroad: The Complete Guide](https://blog.transfez.com/en/indonesian-diaspora-living-abroad-complete-guide/) is a great place to start.


But here is the thing: moving abroad is not just about booking a flight and finding an apartment. There is so much more to it, from navigating visas and culture shock to building a new career and keeping your ties to home strong. This guide breaks it all down for you in a way that is practical, honest, and actually useful.

##


**Who Makes Up the Indonesian Diaspora?**


The Indonesian diaspora is not one single type of person. It is a beautifully diverse group spread across dozens of countries, each with their own reasons for leaving and their own dreams for the future.


###


**1. Overseas Workers (Pekerja Migran)**


*Pekerja migran* , or migrant workers, make up a huge portion of the Indonesian community abroad. Many work in sectors like manufacturing, hospitality, construction, and domestic services, especially in Malaysia, Hong Kong, Taiwan, South Korea, and the Middle East. Their remittances are a lifeline for families back home.


###


**2. Students and Scholars**


Indonesia sends thousands of students abroad every year, chasing degrees and scholarships in countries like Australia, the Netherlands, Japan, and the United States. If you are planning this path, check out[How to Study Abroad from Indonesia: A Complete Guide](https://blog.transfez.com/en/how-to-study-abroad-from-indonesia/) for a step-by-step breakdown.


###


**3. Skilled Professionals and Entrepreneurs**


A growing wave of Indonesian engineers, designers, healthcare workers, and startup founders are building careers in global hubs like Singapore, Germany, and the UK. They are not just employees. Many are founders, freelancers, and thought leaders in their industries.


###


**4. Families and Spouses**


Some Indonesians move abroad because of love, following a partner or spouse to a new country. Others are second-generation diaspora, born overseas to Indonesian parents, still deeply connected to their heritage.


##


**How to Actually Prepare Before You Go**


Preparation is everything. The Indonesians who thrive abroad are almost always the ones who did their homework before landing. Here is what you need to sort out early.


###


**1. Sort Out Your Visa Early**


Your visa determines everything: where you can go, how long you can stay, and what you are legally allowed to do. Work visas, student visas, skilled migrant visas, and tourist visas all have very different requirements. Read up on[How to Get a Visa: A Complete Guide for Beginners](https://blog.transfez.com/en/how-to-get-a-visa/) to understand the process before you commit to anything.


###


**2. Research Your Destination Deeply**


Every country has its own culture, laws, cost of living, and social norms. What works in Jakarta might not fly in Tokyo or Amsterdam. Spend real time researching your destination, not just the tourist highlights but the everyday realities like renting an apartment, opening a bank account, and using public transport.


###


**3. Build Your Financial Safety Net**


Before you go, make sure you have enough savings to cover at least three to six months of living expenses. Unexpected costs always pop up in the first few months abroad, from security deposits to medical expenses to last-minute flights home.


###


**4. Connect with the Indonesian Community There**


Reach out to Indonesian student associations, expat Facebook groups, or community organizations in your destination city before you even arrive. Having a friendly face waiting for you makes the transition so much smoother.


##


**Life Overseas: What No One Tells You**


Living abroad is not a permanent vacation. It is real life, just in a different language and timezone. Here are the honest truths about the diaspora experience that most travel blogs skip over.


###


**1. Culture Shock Is Real and It Takes Time**


Almost every Indonesian who moves abroad goes through culture shock. It usually hits after the initial honeymoon phase fades, somewhere around week two or three. You might feel lonely, homesick, or frustrated by small things. This is completely normal. Give yourself grace and time to adjust.


###


**2. Building a Social Life Takes Effort**


Friendships do not fall into your lap the way they might back home. You need to put yourself out there, join clubs, attend events, say yes to invitations even when you are tired. The effort is worth it, but it does take effort.


###


**3. Language Barriers Are a Real Challenge**


Even if you speak English well, navigating bureaucracy, medical appointments, or workplace culture in a foreign language is exhausting. Consider taking language classes early, even if the country is English-speaking. Local slang and professional vocabulary matter a lot.


###


**4. You Will Miss Indonesian Food**


This sounds like a joke but it is not. The craving for *nasi goreng* , *rendang* , or a simple *warung* meal hits hard. Find the local Indonesian community, because someone always knows where to get the good stuff.


##


**Staying Connected to Home**


Being part of the Indonesian diaspora abroad does not mean leaving your identity behind. In fact, many Indonesians find that living overseas makes them feel more connected to their roots, not less.


###


**1. Send Money Home Regularly and Smartly**


Supporting family back in Indonesia is a priority for most diaspora members. Whether it is helping parents with daily expenses or contributing to a sibling’s education, remittances matter. Learn how to do it efficiently by reading[How to Transfer Money from Abroad to Indonesia](https://blog.transfez.com/en/how-to-transfer-money-from-abroad-to-indonesia/) so you always know your options.


###


**2. Stay Active in the Indonesian Community**


Join your city’s Indonesian community association, attend cultural events, celebrate *Hari Kemerdekaan* on August 17, cook Indonesian food with friends. Keeping those cultural touchpoints alive helps you stay grounded and connected no matter how far from home you are.


###


**3. Keep Indonesian as Your Language at Home**


If you have children or live with other Indonesians, make a point of speaking *Bahasa Indonesia* at home. It is one of the most powerful ways to preserve your identity and pass it on to the next generation.


##


**Building a Career as Part of the Diaspora**


Career growth is one of the biggest motivators for Indonesians moving abroad. And the opportunities are real, but so is the competition.


###


**1. Understand the Local Job Market**


Every country has its own hiring culture. In some places, networking is everything. In others, qualifications and certifications carry the most weight. Research what employers in your field value in your destination country and tailor your resume and LinkedIn accordingly.


###


**2. Get Your Credentials Recognized**


Indonesian degrees and professional certifications are not automatically recognized everywhere. Check whether you need to get your qualifications assessed or whether you need to pass local licensing exams. This is especially important for doctors, lawyers, engineers, and teachers.


###


**3. Consider the Freelance or Remote Option**


Many diaspora Indonesians work remotely for Indonesian or international clients while living abroad. This can be a great way to earn in stronger currencies while enjoying life in a new country. If this is your plan, read up on[How to Work Abroad from Indonesia: A Complete Guide](https://blog.transfez.com/en/how-to-work-abroad-from-indonesia/) for practical tips.


**See Also:**[How to Send Money from Abroad to Indonesia](https://blog.transfez.com/en/how-to-send-money-from-abroad-to-indonesia/)


Being part of the **Indonesian diaspora abroad** is one of the most challenging and rewarding experiences a person can have. It stretches you, teaches you, humbles you, and ultimately makes you stronger. Whether you are just starting to plan your move or you have been living overseas for years, remember that you carry something incredibly valuable with you wherever you go: your identity, your culture, and your connection to a community of millions who are on the same journey. Embrace all of it, and the world really does become your *kampung halaman* .
